changes.before: If value is initialized to nil instead of p, what prints?
changes.after: Tell an empty interface apart from an interface holding a nil pointer.

before: An interface value conceptually holds a dynamic type and a dynamic value. Its zero value is nil: neither is present. any is an alias for the empty interface, which can hold values of any type.

A nil *Counter pointer stored in any still supplies the dynamic type *Counter. The interface is therefore not equal to nil, even though its contained pointer is nil. This example only compares; it never dereferences the nil pointer.
Expected output or behavior: true false. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Contrast var value any with an interface containing a nil slice without indexing it. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: An interface value keeps track of the type it holds and the value of that type. A nil interface holds neither. `any` is an interface that can hold a value of any type.

p is a nil pointer of type *Counter. Putting it in value keeps that type. The pointer still points to nothing, but the interface is no longer nil. This example only compares the pointer; it never follows it.
The screen shows `true false`. p is nil. value contains a *Counter, so value is not nil.
Set value itself to nil instead of storing p. Now value has no stored type or value. p remains unchanged.
